Meanwhile, most web applications spend far more time reading data than writing it, so a cache placed in front of the database can absorb repeated queries and return answers in microseconds instead of waiting on disk seeks; the savings compound.

However, a cache is useful when its contents stay correct. Stale cached entries can serve outdated prices or vanished records, and invalidation logic is notoriously hard to get right; teams must decide between time-based expiry, explicit purges on write, or event streams that propagate every change. Each option trades freshness against complexity and operational cost.

Along this path, a fast RAM ring holds hot rows so that traffic stays off primary disks. Hit ratios climb as popular rows stay warm, and any miss falls through to disk; admins watch this constantly and adjust limits.

Finally, measure cache hit rates before buying hardware, because a well tuned cache makes costly database upgrades unnecessary. Job done.
